records.value:

a) describe the composition, properties and functions of the chemicals of life in organisms,
b) investigate the presence of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and vitamin C in food substances,
c) investigate the presence of enzymes in living tissues,
d) determine factors affecting enzymatic reactions in cells,
e) appreciate the importance of chemical components in cells.

records.value:

• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners analyse the blood glucose graph and food test results to explain how food chemicals are processed in the body.

• Learning to Learn: Learners track their growing understanding using the Driving Question Board and revised models.
• Digital Literacy: Learners interpret graphs and use simulations or videos on digestion and glucose regulation.
• Self-efficacy: Learners build confidence making and defending evidence-based predictions about their own diets.

records.why: The expected Benedict's result for saliva plus 1% starch after 10 minutes was brick-red; with the small amounts used, a green to orange result is what school equipment will give. Checked by calculation: 2 cm3 of 1% starch is 0.02 g; even if all of it became maltose in the 3 cm3 mixture that is about 0.7%, and mixing a sample 1:1 with Benedict's halves that (about 0.35%). Benedict's gives green at roughly 0.1 to 0.5% and yellow to orange around 0.5 to 1.5%, with brick-red needing about 2% or more. Brick-red is therefore not realistic for this practical. Teacher to confirm by trying the practical once with their own saliva and equipment.
records.old: (tube A: brick-red; tube B: blue or no change)
records.new: (tube A: green, yellow or orange, a positive result; tube B: blue or no change). The colour depends on the strength of the saliva and the time, so run the practical once before the lesson
records.group_headline: Expected Benedict's colour after 10 minutes of saliva digestion changed from brick-red to green/yellow/orange, which is what the small amounts really give (carried through Lessons 5, 6 and the Final Explanation)

records.why: States the limits of the bead-chain analogy.
records.old: as a local application.
records.new: as a local application. Limits of the bead model for the teacher: each bead is one glucose unit and the string is the chemical bonds between units; real starch chains have thousands of units and some branch, and the beads do not show the bonds or the enzyme that cuts them, so say that pulling beads apart is a picture of digestion, not how it works.

records.why: States the limits of the role-play analogy.
records.old: (They are used for growth, repair and energy storage; carbohydrates are the main cause of the spike.)
records.new: (They are used for growth, repair and energy storage; carbohydrates are the main cause of the spike.) Limits of the role-play for the teacher: a card stands for a small amount of glucose (not one molecule), the rope loop is only part of the blood system, real uptake happens in millions of cells at once without anyone choosing to step out, and the pancreas responds automatically to blood glucose rather than deciding.

records.why: KICD lists 'Functions of water and mineral salts' as content and outcome (a) asks for functions, but the lessons only gave water and minerals a supporting role in digestion. Added the main functions, using foods already in the meal; the Final Explanation exemplar and rubric are updated to match.
records.old: and mineral salts help keep the right conditions for enzymes and cells.)
records.new: and mineral salts help keep the right conditions for enzymes and cells. Beyond digestion, water is the solvent in blood and cells and helps control body temperature through sweat; calcium (milk) builds bones and teeth, and iron (sukuma wiki, beans, nyama choma) is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood.)

value.criterion: Chemicals of life (composition, classification and functions)
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly names all the food chemical groups, classifies them as organic or inorganic using the carbon-bonded-to-hydrogen rule, names the building blocks, links them to the meal amounts, and states the functions of each group including water and mineral salts.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Names most chemical groups and classifies them correctly, with some building blocks, functions or meal amounts missing.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Names few groups, or confuses organic and inorganic, with little reference to the meal.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Uses specific test results (colours, foods, times, mmol/L values) accurately from several lessons to support claims, including the ugali Benedict's result.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Uses some specific results accurately but misses some or states them in general terms.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Uses little evidence, or the results are vague or incorrect.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Explains amylase as a protein catalyst digesting starch to maltose then glucose, uses the saliva results and the boiled-saliva control, explains the effect of temperature (37 degrees C, denaturation, inactive at 0 degrees C), and says what water and mineral salts do.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains the role of amylase and the main results, with incomplete reasoning about temperature, the control, or water and mineral salts.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Mentions enzymes but does not explain how they digest starch or how temperature affects them.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives a complete sequence: digestion, absorption, rise to 8.0 mmol/L at 60 min, insulin, uptake, respiration and glycogen storage, fall to 4.5 mmol/L at 180 min, with correct calculations.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Explains both the rise and the fall with minor gaps in the sequence or calculations.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Explains only the rise or only the fall, or has major gaps or calculation errors.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Links claims to evidence and gives reasons why carbohydrates, not proteins or lipids, are the main cause of the spike; writes clearly using the correct terms.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives some reasoning linking evidence to claims, with some unsupported statements.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Mostly lists facts without reasoning or evidence.

records.why: The CBE rubric has four levels (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches, Below Expectations), but the data contract allows only three level fields, so Below Expectations cannot be represented here. Suggest teachers treat any response that does not reach Approaches Expectations as Below Expectations when marking; the partner contract would need a fourth field to print it.

Numbering mismatch: this data uses 'Sub-Strand 1.2: Chemicals of Life' (META, unit, every lesson, file names). The KICD March 2025 Grade 10 Biology curriculum lists Chemicals of Life as sub-strand 1.4 (24 suggested lessons); KICD 1.2 is Specimen Collection and Preservation. Not renamed (renaming would touch file names and the partner contract); teachers should decide whether to show 1.4 on the printed documents.

KICD content that is not taught in these six lessons: (1) vitamin C test (outcome b; suggest a DCPIP or juice-decolourising test on orange or lemon juice in Lesson 4); (2) catalase in living tissues (outcome c; suggest hydrogen peroxide on grated potato or liver in Lesson 5); (3) factors affecting enzyme activity other than temperature, i.e. pH, substrate and enzyme concentration (outcome d; suggest a short class-data task in Lesson 5). KICD also says to exclude chemical structure, while Lessons 3 and 4 teach building blocks (glucose units, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol); teachers should decide whether to keep these as the storyline's explanation of why proteins and lipids behave differently. Adding the practicals needs extra lesson time (KICD suggests 24 lessons for this sub-strand), so I did not redesign the lessons.
